# Labels {background-color="#0C234B"}

## The problem with position

```python
data[3, 7]     # ...which well, and which measurement?
```

::: {.fragment}
You wrote that line knowing what column 7 was. Three weeks later you don't, and
neither does anyone reading your code.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Worse: you insert a column at position 2, and every index after it is now
silently wrong. Nothing errors. The numbers just change.
:::

## A DataFrame

```python
wells.loc["320824110593001", "well_depth_ft"]
```

::: {.fragment}
Same lookup, and it says what it means. If a column moves, this keeps working.
If a column disappears, you get a `KeyError` — loudly, at the right place.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**pandas is numpy with labels on it.** Everything you learned last week still
applies underneath.
:::

## The two objects

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`Series`**

One column. Values plus an index.

```python
wells["well_depth_ft"]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`DataFrame`**

A dictionary of Series that share an index.

```python
wells[["site_no", "well_depth_ft"]]
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
One name in brackets gives a Series. A *list* of names gives a DataFrame. That
is the whole rule, and it explains most of the double brackets you'll see.
:::

# Reading data {background-color="#AB0520"}

## `read_csv`, with one precaution

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

ROOT = next(p for p in Path.cwd().parents if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists())
wells = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data" / "tucson_basin_wells.csv",
                    dtype={"site_no": str})
```

::: {.fragment}
`dtype={"site_no": str}` is not decoration. Site numbers are 15-digit
identifiers; pandas would read them as integers, drop leading zeros, and break
every join you make later — without a warning.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Walking up to find the repo root beats counting `../..`, which works right up
until you move the file.
:::

## Four things to check, every time

::: {.incremental}
1. `df.dtypes` — is anything a string that should be a number?
2. `df.isna().sum()` — how much is missing, and where?
3. `df.describe()` — do the numbers look physical?
4. `len(df)` — did you get the number of rows you expected?
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Thirty seconds. It catches the mistakes that otherwise survive all the way into
a figure.
:::

## What that finds in the real thing

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 10
import pandas as pd

# a slice of the real inventory, hardcoded so it runs in the browser
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site_no": ["320000110555701", "320001110584201", "320002110584001",
                "320002110584201", "320004110572601"],
    "well_depth_ft": [61.0, 110.0, 835.0, None, 397.0],
    "land_surface_elev_ft": [2675.0, 2698.0, 2701.0, 2699.0, 2662.0],
})
print(wells.dtypes)
print()
print(wells.isna().sum())
```

::: {.fragment}
One well in five has no depth on file. In the full inventory it is 184 of 1,693
— and every filter you write on depth will silently drop them.
:::

## Selecting columns

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 8
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site_no": ["A", "B", "C"],
    "well_depth_ft": [61.0, 110.0, 835.0],
    "land_surface_elev_ft": [2675.0, 2698.0, 2701.0],
})

print(type(wells["well_depth_ft"]))         # Series
print(type(wells[["well_depth_ft"]]))       # DataFrame
print(wells[["site_no", "well_depth_ft"]])
```

## Your turn: land surface in metres

Add a column `land_surface_elev_m`, then find the mean well depth in feet.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_col
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site_no": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    "well_depth_ft": [61.0, 110.0, 835.0, 397.0],
    "land_surface_elev_ft": [2675.0, 2698.0, 2701.0, 2662.0],
})
FEET_TO_M = 0.3048
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_col
wells["land_surface_elev_m"] = ______
mean_depth = ______
print(wells)
print(f"mean depth: {mean_depth:.1f} ft")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_col"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Assigning to a column name that doesn't exist creates it. The arithmetic is
elementwise, exactly like numpy.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_col"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
wells["land_surface_elev_m"] = wells["land_surface_elev_ft"] * FEET_TO_M
mean_depth = wells["well_depth_ft"].mean()
```

`350.8` ft. Note that `.mean()` **skips missing values silently** — with a
`None` in the column you would get the mean of the three that remain, and no
indication that you did.
:::
:::

# `.loc` and `.iloc` {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Labels vs. positions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`.loc[]`**

By **label** — the index value and the column name.

```python
wells.loc["320824110593001",
          "well_depth_ft"]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`.iloc[]`**

By **integer position**, like numpy.

```python
wells.iloc[3, 1]
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
They look interchangeable on a fresh DataFrame only because its index happens to
be `0, 1, 2, ...`. Set a real index and they part company immediately.
:::

## The slice trap

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 7
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]})

print("iloc[2:5] ->", len(df.iloc[2:5]), "rows")
print("loc[2:5]  ->", len(df.loc[2:5]), "rows")
```

::: {.fragment}
**`.loc` slices are inclusive of the endpoint.** Every other slice in Python is
half-open. This is genuinely inconsistent, it is not going to change, and it
catches everyone exactly once.
:::

## Your turn: pull one well

Using `.loc`, get the depth and land surface elevation of well `"C-22"`.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_loc
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "well_depth_ft": [61.0, 110.0, 835.0, 397.0],
    "land_surface_elev_ft": [2675.0, 2698.0, 2701.0, 2662.0],
}, index=["A-14", "B-07", "C-22", "D-03"])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_loc
one_well = ______
print(one_well)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_loc"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`.loc` takes rows first, then columns: `.loc[row_label, column_labels]`. You
want both columns, so pass a list of the two names — or just the row label on
its own.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_loc"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
one_well = wells.loc["C-22", ["well_depth_ft", "land_surface_elev_ft"]]
```

`wells.loc["C-22"]` alone works too and gives the whole row. Naming the columns
explicitly is worth the extra characters when the table is wide — it documents
what you actually needed.
:::
:::

## Your turn: `.loc` or `.iloc`?

The index here is site numbers, not integers. Get the **third row** by position,
and the well `"C-22"` by name.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_which
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "well_depth_ft": [61.0, 110.0, 835.0, 397.0],
}, index=["A-14", "B-07", "C-22", "D-03"])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_which
third_row = wells.______[2]
by_name = wells.______["C-22"]
print(f"third row: {third_row['well_depth_ft']}")
print(f"C-22:      {by_name['well_depth_ft']}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_which"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

"Third row" is a position. `"C-22"` is a label. One accessor each.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_which"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
third_row = wells.iloc[2]
by_name = wells.loc["C-22"]
```

Both return `835.0` here — because C-22 *is* the third row. That coincidence is
exactly why this distinction is easy to get away with being vague about, right
up until the day you sort the table.
:::
:::

## Wrap up {.smaller}

::: {.kicker}
What you did today
:::

- A DataFrame is numpy with labels, and labels survive a column moving
- One name gives a Series; a list of names gives a DataFrame
- `dtype={"site_no": str}` for anything that is an identifier, not a number
- `.loc` is labels, `.iloc` is positions, and `.loc` slices include the endpoint
